title: Japan to Look at Conditions in Wild Animal Cafes
paragraphs: Animal cafes, where customers can drink coffee while interacting with animals, have become a popular attraction in Japan, particularly among tourists. Now, the Japanese government has started looking more closely at how these businesses treat their animals, especially those that keep wild species such as owls and otters.

In September 2026, Japan's Environment Ministry began its first nationwide survey of animal cafes. The survey will look at how many of these cafes exist, which animals they keep, the conditions in which the animals live and how visitors are allowed to interact with them. Although the survey also includes cafes with cats and dogs, it is especially relevant for the growing number of businesses that keep owls, otters, reptiles and other wild animals. Officials will also check whether the cafes are following animal welfare laws, for instance by making sure that animals have enough space. If any cafes appear to be breaking the rules, on-site inspections may follow.

At present, Japan has no rules designed specifically for animal cafes. According to Takuya Ishikawa, an official at the Environment Ministry, there are also no specific standards for handling many exotic species. He added that there has been strong public interest in the issue, including from animal welfare groups.

Research has raised a number of concerns. When researchers visited 25 animal cafes near Tokyo, they found more than 1,700 animals on display, and 27% of them belonged to threatened species. More than 90% of the cafes displayed animals that were considered to be at high risk of injury through contact with people. In addition, samples from four cafes tested positive for a dangerous type of E. coli bacteria that can cause serious illness.
There are also concerns about the wildlife trade. According to a report by the World Wildlife Fund, Japan was the world's second-largest importer of live reptiles and mammals by value in 2024.

Some cafe operators have welcomed the review. Syaina Nozaki, who manages a cafe for rescued owls and otters in Kamakura, said Japan is clearly lagging behind in animal welfare regulation. Nozaki hopes that new rules will help separate responsible businesses from those that only care about making money.
